xiao-sense.name: Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, pre-soldered
xiao-sense.what: The brain: a computer the size of a thumbnail, with a camera. "Pre-soldered" means its legs are already on.

oled.name: Seeed Grove OLED 0.96"
oled.what: The screen. As big as a postage stamp.

grove-cable.name: Grove to jumper-pin cable
grove-cable.what: Four coloured wires from the screen to the breadboard.

breadboard.name: Half-size breadboard
breadboard.what: A board full of holes. Push parts in and they connect.

jumpers.name: Jumper wires, male to male
jumpers.what: Short wires with a pin on each end.

usb-cable.name: USB-C cable that carries data
usb-cable.what: Some cables only charge. One that came with a phone usually works.

power-bank.name: USB power bank or phone charger
power-bank.what: Power without the computer. You probably have one.

lens.name: Plano-convex lens, 20 mm wide, about 50 mm focal length

mirror.name: First-surface mirror, about 25 by 20 mm
mirror.what: A mirror with the shiny part on the front.

beam-splitter.name: Beam splitter, 30 by 30 mm, 50/50
beam-splitter.what: Glass that is half mirror and half window.

bno085.name: Adafruit BNO085 (product 4754)
bno085.what: A motion sensor. It knows which way it points.

qwiic-cable.name: STEMMA QT (Qwiic) to jumper-pin cable
qwiic-cable.what: Plugs into the motion sensor. No soldering.

mics.name: 4 INMP441 microphones, pins already soldered
mics.what: Check the listing says the pins are soldered on.

frames.name: Glasses you do not mind taping things to

lipo.name: LiPo battery, 500 mAh, with a protection circuit

switch.name: Small slide switch and thin wire

display-glasses.name: Display glasses with a USB-C cable (Rokid Max, Xreal Air, Viture), used
display-glasses.what: A two-eye screen you wear. It plugs into the iPhone.

respeaker-flex.name: Seeed reSpeaker Flex XVF3800 Linear-4 with XIAO ESP32S3
respeaker-flex.what: Four microphones on a strip, with a chip that finds voice direction itself.

jumpers-fm.name: Jumper wires, female to male, 15 cm
jumpers-fm.what: A socket on one end and a pin on the other. They reach from the microphones to the breadboard.

ruler.name: A 15 cm ruler, or a strip of stiff card that long
ruler.what: The microphones are taped along it.

cap.name: A cap with a stiff brim
cap.what: Carries the ruler and the breadboard until you solder.

recipes.name: Display glasses with a sensor pod
recipes.summary: Bought display glasses show captions beside whoever is speaking. A small pod you build tells the iPhone where voices are.
recipes.notes: The display glasses plug into the iPhone and need an iPhone that sends video over USB-C (iPhone 15 or later, except iPhone Air and 16e). The pod's little screen is optional but makes the checks much easier.

recipes.name: Display glasses with a homemade microphone strip
recipes.summary: The bought microphone strip, made yourself: four small microphones taped along a ruler. Cheaper, no soldering, and the camera adds how far away the speaker is.
recipes.notes: Nobody has built it yet. The direction sums for a row are tested on simulated sound, and the firmware builds, but it has not run on a board. A straight row of microphones tells left from right, not ahead from behind. The little screen is optional but makes the checks much easier. The display glasses need an iPhone that sends video over USB-C (iPhone 15 or later, except iPhone Air and 16e).

recipes.name: One-eye caption glasses
recipes.summary: Captions floating in front of one eye, with the glasses knowing where each voice is and how far away the speaker is.
recipes.notes: Everything on one board. The one-eye screen shows the speaker's number and which side they are on; it cannot float a caption beside them.

recipes.name: One-eye caption glasses with the ready-made strip
recipes.summary: The homemade floating screen in front of one eye, with the bought strip doing the listening. Less wiring than four microphones, more soldering than the other strip recipes.
recipes.notes: Written from Seeed's documents; nobody has built it. The firmware asks the strip's chip for the voice angle and builds cleanly, but has not run on this board. Not yet checked: which end of the strip counts as 0 degrees, and whether the chip needs its sound clock running. A straight row of microphones cannot tell ahead from behind. The screen and the motion sensor are both soldered to the same four legs of the small board, because this board has no plugs for them; that step is unchecked. The main board's size is not published, so the lessons put it on a cap or collar. No camera on this board, so no distance.

recipes.name: One-eye caption glasses with a microphone strip
recipes.summary: Everything homemade: the floating screen in front of one eye, and four microphones in a row along the top of the frames. The row is easier to get working than microphones at four corners.
recipes.notes: Nobody has built it yet. The direction sums for a row are tested on simulated sound and the firmware builds, but it has not run on a board. A straight row of microphones tells left from right, not ahead from behind. The one-eye screen shows the speaker's number and which side they are on; it cannot float a caption beside them.

recipes.name: Display glasses with a ready-made microphone strip
recipes.summary: As the sensor pod, with a bought four-microphone strip that finds voice direction itself. Less wiring.
recipes.notes: Written from Seeed's documents; nobody has built it. The firmware asks the strip's chip for the voice angle over I2C (address 0x2C, DOA_VALUE) and builds cleanly, but has not run on this board. Not yet checked: which end of the strip counts as 0 degrees, whether the chip needs its sound clock running, where best to solder the motion sensor (the board has no plug for it), the size of the main board, and whether a small battery can be fitted. A straight line of microphones cannot tell ahead from behind. The display glasses need an iPhone that sends video over USB-C (iPhone 15 or later, except iPhone Air and 16e).

recipes.name: Caption screen
recipes.summary: A small screen that shows HearAura's captions. The place to start: about an hour, no soldering.
recipes.notes: Uses the simplest part of the firmware, so it has the best chance of working first time. A plain XIAO ESP32-S3 (no camera) works too.

recipes.name: Table captions with the ready-made strip
recipes.summary: The strip and a small screen stand on the table. The screen shows what is said, each speaker's number, and which side they are on. Nothing to wear.
recipes.notes: Written from Seeed's documents; nobody has built it. The firmware asks the strip's chip for the voice angle and builds cleanly, but has not run on this board. Not yet checked: which end of the strip counts as 0 degrees, and whether the chip needs its sound clock running. A straight row of microphones cannot tell ahead from behind. The screen's four wires are soldered to the small board, because this board has no plug for it; where best to solder them is unchecked too. A table does not turn, so no motion sensor is needed.

recipes.name: Display glasses with the strip on the table
recipes.summary: The quickest way to captions beside each speaker: bought display glasses, and the bought strip standing on the table in front of you. No soldering, nothing to build onto the glasses.
recipes.notes: Written from Seeed's documents; nobody has built it. The firmware asks the strip's chip for the voice angle and builds cleanly, but has not run on this board. Not yet checked: which end of the strip counts as 0 degrees, and whether the chip needs its sound clock running. A straight row of microphones cannot tell ahead from behind. Sides are measured from the strip, not from your head: they are right while you sit behind the strip facing the same way it does, and drift when you turn. The display glasses need an iPhone that sends video over USB-C (iPhone 15 or later, except iPhone Air and 16e).
